message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
Here is what I recall of "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team", from memory and without rechecking. Wording is approximate. I've marked where I'm less sure.

**Opening**
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice is what slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Every claim has earned some weight, whether from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes.
- Part of that weight comes from the evidence and part from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues with years in an area have usually been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- When an experienced person states something with confidence, that confidence is itself evidence, because it reflects checks they've already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly, but they are not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions can look careful while adding little, and can undermine good work.
- *Example:* a colleague reports a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If they've managed that supplier for years, take the report as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2. Take in what was said before you answer**
- Make sure you've taken in a message and show that you have: restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it.
- This is "not politeness". It is how a conversation moves forward instead of circling.
- Start from what you agree with: find the part that's right, say so, and extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement put people on the defensive and cost more time than they save.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step.
- *Example:* a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. The reply confirms the direction, picks up the actionable points, and says the budget will follow "in due course."

**§3. Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has already been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go back to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and can signal distrust of colleagues.
- The value of a shared record is that the team builds on it together.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into "private versions of the truth" and can't act.
- *Example:* a report is summarised as "costs fell 12%." Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

**§4. Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions the evidence settles and some it leaves less certain. Mark which is which, then keep moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block dependent decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer. It can be revisited, whereas a question left hanging tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping questions open because one more check feels safer, is "the more common one in careful people". It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed and save energy for live questions.
- *Example:* a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Problems there can be handled as they arise.

**§5. Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues and those from other parts of the organisation see things differently. That can be valuable if their time is used well.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team already knows.
- When asking for a check, give context: what you've concluded, where you think the risks are, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster.
- When you're the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well founded and the moment is right.
- A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.

**§6. Make your moves where they will land well**
- Before taking a step you can see is good, check it fits with what the owners of the area have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating them. Make the call once the direction is confirmed. Release results when they're ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked and costs more than a short conversation beforehand.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your own position, and owners see considerations you can't. Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This is not a licence to wait indefinitely. Small routine steps don't need sign-off, but for steps that affect others the default is to check first, then act together.
- *Example:* rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether, and how, they'd like it restructured.

**§7. Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other.
- I recall these pairs:
  - Overclaiming / second-guessing
  - Inventing a flaw (to look rigorous) / overlooking one
  - Closing too early / keeping open too long
  - Abandoning a line / relitigating one
  - Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively (disputing experienced colleagues)
  - Acting alone / waiting too long
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- "When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one."

**A last word**
- This is not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, and an agreed direction. "Trust those. They are how good work gets done together."

**Less confident:**
- the exact order of the §7 pairs and the precise glosses attached to each;
- the exact wording of the §6 sequence (drafts, calls, releases);
- whether §4 explicitly called keeping questions open "the more common one in careful people." I believe it did.
